newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish c.bank mulls reserves for govt paper swap.
newsitem.headline: Polish c.bank mulls reserves for govt paper swap.

text.p: Poland's central bank wants to swap some of its hard currency reserves for zloty-bonds with the treasury and use the bonds in its money market drainages, a senior central bank official said.

Jacek Osinski, deputy head of the bank's monetary policy department said the government could in turn use the currencies to buy, for example, long term U.S. bonds, maturing when Poland would need the currencies most to pay its debt installments.

"The central bank has offered the finance ministry to use part of the official reserves in swap transations for zloty bonds, which it would use in outright sales to sterilise the market," Osinski told Reuters.
In July, the National Bank of Poland had $17.78 billion of hard currency reserves, up $2.83 billion from the end of 1995.
"The swaps would be a long-term policy, done when needed to sterilise fast reserve growth," he said.

He said such swaps could take place for instance with big privatisations, such as the telecommunications monopoly (TPSA), to eliminate the multiplier effect of money supply growth as a result of large one-off foreign capital injection.

"Imagine Poland sells a 25 percent stake in TPSA and gets a lot of money because it is a big company. But it gets the cash now, while the bulk of our debt payments is after the year 2003, and that is when we need it," said Osinski.
"...the cash only causes a jump in market liquidity, forcing the NBP to sterilise it to avoid the monetary shock with all its negative effects," he said.
The bulk of Poland's foreign debt repayment of over $6 billion annually is scheduled for the years 2004-2008.

Osinski said the National Bank of Poland's simulations on 1996 data showed such transactions could, depending on the maturity of the zloty paper used, be either neutral or profitable from the point of view of the treasury.
He said for the simulations the NBP used 52-week T-bills, as well as fixed interest five-year bonds and variable-interest 10-year paper, but that deals could be done on other instruments as well.
He said the operations would boost the domestic public debt, but stressed they would do so gradually, allowing for the elimination of uncomfortable debt payment pile-ups.
The finance ministry declined comment on the idea.
